t.2.102.1: Perceiving that Rāma was angry, Vasiṣṭha replied: "Jābāli too knows the coming and going of this world; but it was out of a wish to turn you back that he spoke these words to you."
t.2.102.2: Learn from me, O lord of the world, this account of the origin of the world. In the beginning all was water alone, and within it the earth was fashioned. Then arose the self-existent Brahmā together with the deities.
t.2.102.3: Then, having become a boar, he raised up the earth, and together with his sons of perfected self he created the entire world.
t.2.102.4: Brahmā, who arose from space, is eternal, everlasting and imperishable. From him Marīci was born, and from Marīci came Kaśyapa, his son.
t.2.102.5: Vivasvān was born of Kaśyapa, and Manu, son of Vivasvān, is remembered as Vaivasvata. He was formerly a Prajāpati, a lord of creatures, and Ikṣvāku was the son of Manu.
t.2.102.6: Know that Ikṣvāku, to whom this prosperous earth was first given by Manu, was the first king in Ayodhyā.
t.2.102.7: The son of Ikṣvāku was the glorious one renowned as Kukṣi. Then to Kukṣi was born a son, the heroic Vikukṣi.
t.2.102.8: Vikukṣi's son was the mighty and greatly radiant Bāṇa, and Bāṇa's son was the strong-armed Anaraṇya of great renown.
t.2.102.10: From Anaraṇya was born the mighty-armed King Pṛthu; from that Pṛthu arose the great king Triśaṅku. That hero, by virtue of his truthful word, went to heaven in his own body.
t.2.102.9: While this great king Anaraṇya, the best of the virtuous, reigned, there was no drought, no famine, nor any thief at all.
t.2.102.11: To Triśaṅku was born a son, the greatly renowned Dhundhumāra; from Dhundhumāra was born the greatly splendid Yuvanāśva.
t.2.102.12: The illustrious Māndhātā was born as the son of Yuvanāśva; and from Māndhātā was born the greatly radiant Susaṃdhi.
t.2.102.13: From Susaṃdhi, moreover, were born two sons, Dhruvasaṃdhi and Prasenajit; and from Dhruvasaṃdhi was born the glorious Bharata, slayer of enemies.
t.2.102.14: From the mighty-armed Bharata was born one named Asita, against whom these rival kings arose as enemies: the Haihayas, the Tālajaṅghas, and the valiant Śaśabindus.
t.2.102.16: There was a Bhārgava named Cyavana who had taken refuge on the Himavant. Kālindī approached that seer and saluted him respectfully.
t.2.102.15: Having arrayed himself against all of them in battle, the king was driven into exile, and he became a sage, delighting in life on a lovely, excellent mountain. His two wives were pregnant, so tradition says.
t.2.102.17: The brahmin spoke to her as she sought a boon for the birth of a son. Then the queen returned home and gave birth to a son.
t.2.102.18: Her co-wife, seeking to destroy the child in her womb, gave her poison; and because he was born together with that very poison, he became Sagara.
t.2.102.20: We have heard that Sagara had a son named Asamañja; but because he was a doer of wicked deeds, he was cast out by his father while still living.
t.2.102.19: He was the king named Sagara who, after performing a sacrifice, had the ocean dug out, the ocean that terrifies these creatures with its surging force at the change of the moon.
t.2.102.21: Asamañja had a valiant son named Aṃśumān. Dilīpa was the son of Aṃśumān, and Bhagīratha was the son of Dilīpa.
t.2.102.22: From Bhagīratha was born Kakutstha, by whom his descendants are known as the Kākutsthas; and to Kakutstha was born a son, Raghu, by whom the line is called Rāghava.
t.2.102.23: The son of Raghu was the splendid Kalmāṣapāda, who grew mighty and became a devourer of men; he was renowned on earth as Saudāsa.
t.2.102.24: The son of Kalmāṣapāda was renowned as Śaṅkhaṇa, who, having encountered that might, perished together with his army.
t.2.102.25: To Śaṅkhaṇa was born a son, the valiant and glorious Sudarśana; Sudarśana's son was Agnivarṇa, and Agnivarṇa's son was Śīghraga.
t.2.102.26: The son of Śīghraga was Maru; the son of Maru was Praśuśruka; and to Praśuśruka was born a son, Ambarīṣa of great splendor.
t.2.102.27: Ambarīṣa's son was Nahuṣa, whose valor was true; and Nahuṣa's son was Nābhāga, supremely righteous.
t.2.102.28: Aja and Suvrata were both sons of Nābhāga, and the son of Aja was the righteous-souled King Daśaratha.
t.2.102.29: You, renowned by the name Rāma, are his eldest heir; therefore take up your own kingdom and watch over the world, O king.
t.2.102.31: You, then, ought not today to abandon the eternal family law of the Rāghavas, which is your own; O greatly renowned one, rule like your father over this earth, abounding in jewels and rich in kingdoms.
t.2.102.30: For among all the Ikṣvākus it is the firstborn who becomes king; the younger son stands below the firstborn, and it is the eldest who is consecrated to the kingship.
